newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea braces for more student violence.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea braces for more student violence.

text.p: The South Korean capital was braced for its third day of street violence on Sunday as students prepared to march in protest against President Kim Young-sam's refusal to reveal election spending abuses.
Students were gathering on campuses around town and planning to converge on city hall, local media said. But they were expected to meet heavy police resistance.
More than 10,000 South Korean students went on the rampage in Seoul on Saturday.
Chanting "Bring down Kim Young-sam" and "Reveal the Election Funds", they hurled Molotov cocktails at riot police in skirmishes across wide areas of the capital.
Some of the fiercest clashes occurred outside the luxury Shilla Hotel.
Tourist buses and taxis ran a gauntlet of rock- throwing protesters to get in and out and occasionally had to ferry terrified passengers at high speed across sheets of fire set by petrol bombs.

South Korea's student movement, which seemed to have been crushed when 151 student leaders were jailed following a campus uprising last year, has won a new lease on life thanks to the opposition's campaign to force Kim to come clean on his election spending.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics maintains Kim's campaign was partly bankrolled by the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group and his disgraced predecessor, Roh Tae-woo, and far exceeded the legal spending limit.
Analysts on Sunday said President Kim would have to move swiftly to calm public outrage by implementing political reform in June during an extraordinary session of parliament.
The date for the session is still under negotiation between ruling and opposition parties.

On Friday, President Kim apologised on live television for widespread spending abuses, but sparked a new furore as he challanged the opposition to clean up politics or face his "grave decision". He did not elaborate.

The leading Chosun Ilbo newspaper on Sunday reported that Kim Jong-pil, leader of the smaller opposition United Liberal Democrats, could push for the resignation of President Kim unless he cooperates with a parliamentary investigation and testifies on his own irregularities.
Political science professor at Yonsei University Moon Chung-in said everyone was still guessing what "grave decision" meant.
"It could be a moderate reform or a political suicide to take down all three Kims," he said.

The National Congress elected Kim Dae-jung as its standard-bearer in December presidential polls and Kim Jong-pil is so far the only candidate for the United Liberal Democrats declared to run. President Kim's single term ends in February.
"President Kim could have a card to bring down his opponents and boost his ruling party candidate," Moon said.
